```
A consumer handles 100 requests per second, and for an hour the producer sends 150 per second into an unbounded queue with no backpressure. What follows?

A. The producer is slowed down automatically, so latency stays flat and no work is lost.
B. Excess requests are dropped at the entry point, so the accepted work still completes on time.
C. Throughput falls in proportion to the overload, so the system degrades gently rather than failing.
D. The queue grows without limit, so latency climbs for every request until memory runs out.
E. I don't know
```
cues: D is the only option that mentions the queue named in the stem, and 'grows without limit' restates 'unbounded'
A, B and C all describe benign outcomes (no loss, on time, degrades gently); D is the only negative one, so the stem's 'unbounded' and 'no backpressure' point toward it
A contradicts the stem's 'no backpressure', which makes it easy to rule out

Q1 · failure
An agent runs a 10-step tool loop, and each step on its own succeeds 95% of the time. You run it 1,000 times in production. What do you see?

A. Roughly 5% of runs end wrong, the same rate as a single step.
B. Roughly 0.5% of runs end wrong, fewer than any single step alone.
C. Roughly 40% of runs end wrong, though every step passes its own test.
D. Roughly 40% of runs fail at step one, and the rest finish correctly.
E. I don't know
cues: The 40% figure appears in both C and D, so a test-wise student would narrow to those two.
C's concessive clause ('though every step passes its own test') echoes the stem's 'each step on its own succeeds' and signals a counterintuitive 'gotcha' answer, the kind item writers favor.
D's 'the rest finish correctly' is an absolute claim that reads as implausible, which leaves C as the more defensible of the pair.

A payment API has no idempotency key. A client sends "charge $50", the server charges the card, but the response is lost and the client times out and retries once. What does the customer see?

A. One $50 charge, because the server rejects the retry as a duplicate
B. No charge, because the timeout rolls back the first charge
C. Two $50 charges, because the server runs both requests in full
D. One $50 charge, because the retry waits for the first one to commit
E. I don't know
cues: All four options share the same 'outcome, because mechanism' structure and are similar in length and register
No option echoes the stem's wording distinctively or hedges differently
Weak cue: A and D share the same outcome ('One $50 charge'), so a test-wise student might eliminate both, leaving B or C. This does not single out one option

Which of these describes an idempotent operation?

A. Every call with the same input returns the same response
B. The system makes sure the operation runs exactly once
C. Repeating it changes nothing beyond what the first call did
D. It can be retried only after the first attempt has failed
E. I don't know
cues: All four options are similar in length and phrasing (8–11 words)
All use the same plain declarative register with no hedging
None is noticeably more specific than the others
B repeats 'operation' from the question, but the echo is weak and generic
A and C share 'call', so neither stands out
D is slightly longer, but its restrictive 'only after' wording makes it less attractive, not more

A. Judge win-rate falls week by week while answers get shorter and humans rate them better.
B. Judge win-rate stays flat week by week because the judge scores most candidate pairs as ties.
C. Judge win-rate climbs week by week while answers get longer and humans rate them no better.
D. Judge win-rate climbs week by week and human ratings climb with it, tracking it closely.

D's 'tracking it closely' adds slight emphasis but is not a strong enough cue to pick it

Q1 · mechanism
In a pairwise LLM-as-judge eval, why is each comparison run twice, with the order of the two answers swapped?

A. The judge samples randomly, so two runs are averaged to cut the variance from temperature.
B. The judge tends to favour the longer answer, so swapping order cancels out the length advantage.
C. The judge tends to favour its own model's output, so swapping order hides which model wrote which.
D. The judge tends to favour an answer for its position, so only verdicts that survive the swap count.
E. I don't know
cues: B, C and D share the same template ('The judge tends to favour X, so swapping order...'), and A is the odd one out, so the choice narrows to B/C/D by pattern alone
Within that set, only D names a bias ('position') that maps directly onto the question's 'order of the two answers swapped'; B's length and C's self-preference have no surface link to ordering
D's ending, 'only verdicts that survive the swap count', echoes 'swapped' from the question and reads as the most procedurally specific

question:
Q1 · mechanism
An app pastes a fetched web page into its prompt, and the model then follows an instruction hidden in that page. What lets that happen?

A. The page's text is run as code by the model's tool layer before the prompt is built
B. The model treats retrieved text as data unless it is longer than the system prompt
C. Instructions and untrusted data reach the model as one token stream, with no separate channel
D. The page's text overwrites the stored system prompt in the provider's session memory
E. I don't know
cues: Only option phrased as a general principle ('one token stream, with no separate channel') rather than a narrow, oddly specific mechanism
Uses precise technical vocabulary ('untrusted data', 'token stream') that matches the question's framing better than the other options
Its trailing appositive clause ('with no separate channel') adds the elaboration typical of a carefully written correct answer
Distractors carry give-away absurdities a test-wise student can rule out: B's arbitrary 'longer than the system prompt' condition, D's 'overwrites', A's 'run as code'
Lengths are roughly equal, so the cue is weak and comes from register and precision, not length

question:
Q1 · consequence
A dependency starts timing out on a small share of its requests, and the three service layers above it each retry failed calls a few times. Why does this usually make the outage bigger rather than smaller?

A. The retries hide the errors from monitoring, so the outage spreads before anyone notices it.
B. The retries repeat non-idempotent writes, so corrupted data spreads the failure to other services.
C. The retries multiply across layers, so the struggling dependency gets far more load than before.
D. The retries add the same small extra load at each layer, so total load rises only slightly.
E. I don't know
cues: All four options share the same 'The retries X, so Y' template and are similar in length and register
C and D both echo 'layers' from the question, so the echo doesn't single out either one
D can be ruled out because 'rises only slightly' contradicts the question's premise that the outage gets bigger, but that only narrows the field and doesn't point to the answer
B uses a more technical term ('non-idempotent'), but it isn't more precise or hedged in a way that marks it as the key

A. Up to 3 requests
B. Up to 9 requests
C. Up to 27 requests
D. Up to 81 requests
E. I don't know
cues: All options share identical 'Up to N requests' phrasing and length
Values form a uniform geometric sequence (3, 9, 27, 81) with no option singled out by format
Three hops with 3 attempts each lets a test-wise student pick C by echoing the numbers in the stem, but that requires doing the computation, not reading a surface cue
